lead: Cloud computing moves spending from buying servers to renting them by the hour, and moves control from your building to a provider's. That trade is the whole chapter: the same contract that gives elasticity and global reach also gives lock-in and a bill that can move without your data moving. Use this ledger when you choose a deployment model, size a budget, or design for failure.
prereq: You need: the five essential characteristics from Chapter 1.3, so each benefit can be matched to the characteristic that produces it.

sections.h3: Benefits: capital cost becomes operating cost

blocks.text: Capital expenditure (capex) is money spent once on an asset you own: a server, a rack, a generator. Operating expenditure (opex) is money spent as you consume a service. The cloud turns the first into the second. Instead of buying a server for a peak you may never reach, you rent capacity by the hour or the month.

Elasticity removes over-provisioning. Over-provisioning means buying for the busiest hour and leaving the machine idle for the rest. A ticket site that sees a Tatkal rush at 10 a.m. can add instances for that hour and remove them after. You pay for the demand you had, not for the demand you feared.

The start is faster because there is no procurement cycle. A team can create a database and a web server in minutes, not weeks. Global reach comes from regions: a provider already runs data centres in many places, so you can place a copy near your users without building a site.

The provider also carries routine work: patching the hypervisor, replacing failed disks, keeping redundant power. Your team can spend its time on the product, not on the machine room. These gains are the benefits side of the ledger; each one creates a matching risk on the other side.

sections.h3: Risks and challenges: the other side of the same contract

blocks.text: Vendor lock-in means leaving is expensive. It grows from proprietary APIs, special data formats, and egress fees. If your code calls one provider's queue by name, moving to another provider is a rewrite, not a copy.

Data security and privacy stay your job. The provider secures the building and the hypervisor; you secure your accounts, keys and data. A shared disk is split by software, so tenant isolation must hold. Tenant isolation means one customer's virtual machine cannot read another's memory or disk.

Regulatory compliance and data location add a legal risk. Some regulators require certain data to stay inside the country. The provider may have a region there, but you must choose it and prove it in an audit.

Outages happen, and dependency on the link is real. A provider outage can stop your service; a cut in your office fibre can stop your access even when the cloud is healthy. Latency grows with distance, so a region far from users adds delay to every request.

The bill can surprise. Egress charges are payments for data leaving the provider's network; storage charges continue for data you keep but do not read. Low-level control is limited: you cannot tune the physical network or the host kernel in a public cloud. A skills gap is common: the team must learn identity, networking and cost controls that the old data centre hid.

sections.h3: Threat types and the benefit-to-risk ledger

blocks.text: Four threat types appear in almost every cloud risk register. A data breach is unauthorised access to stored data. Account hijack is stolen credentials used to run resources in your name. An insecure interface is an API or console with weak authentication or missing input checks. Denial of service is traffic that exhausts a service so real users cannot reach it. Attack vectors and controls belong to Unit 6; cost models belong to Unit 4.
Use a ledger, not a list. For every benefit, name the risk it creates and the mitigation that keeps the risk acceptable.

blocks.text: One category check: egress charges are a cost risk, not a security risk. They can make a bill unaffordable, but they do not expose data. Exams mark the category.

examples.question: A startup stores 1 TB of photos in the cloud at ₹2 per GB per month and serves 3 TB of downloads each month at ₹6.50 per GB. (a) Compute the monthly bill and the share of it caused by downloads. (b) If a video goes viral and downloads double, compute the new bill.
steps: Storage volume = 1 TB = 1,024 GB. Storage cost = 1,024 GB × ₹2 per GB = ₹2,048 per month.
Download volume = 3 TB = 3,072 GB. Download cost = 3,072 GB × ₹6.50 per GB = ₹19,968 per month.
Download share = 19,968 ÷ 22,016 = 0.906976... = 90.7% to one decimal place.

If downloads double, download volume = 6 TB = 6,144 GB. New download cost = 6,144 GB × ₹6.50 per GB = ₹39,936. New total = ₹2,048 + ₹39,936 = ₹41,984 per month. Stored data is still 1 TB, so storage cost is unchanged.
examples.answer: The monthly bill is ₹22,016, of which 90.7% is download; if downloads double the bill becomes ₹41,984 and storage cost stays at ₹2,048.

traps: Answering only the benefits when the question says benefits and risks; the examiner wants both columns.
Calling egress charges a security risk; they are a cost risk, and the category carries marks.
Saying cloud removes all management; the provider manages the layers below the service boundary, you manage above it.
Confusing capital cost with operating cost; capex is bought once, opex is consumed.
Forgetting that data location is a compliance risk, not only a latency issue.

quiz.q: Define capex and opex in one line each.
quiz.a: Capex is money spent once on an asset you own; opex is money spent as you consume a service.
Over-provisioning buys for peak demand and leaves capacity idle. Elasticity adds and removes capacity with demand, so the bill follows actual use.

quiz.q: A team stores 500 GB at ₹3 per GB per month and transfers 1 TB out at ₹8 per GB. Compute the monthly bill and the egress share.
quiz.a: Storage = 500 × ₹3 = ₹1,500. Egress = 1 TB = 1,024 GB × ₹8 = ₹8,192. Total = ₹9,692. Egress share = 8,192 ÷ 9,692 = 84.5% to one decimal place.

quiz.q: A manager says the cloud is riskier because data sits on shared hardware. Give one counter-argument and one genuine risk that remains.
quiz.a: Counter: tenant isolation and encryption can keep shared hardware safe, and the provider may patch faster than a small team. Genuine risk: misconfigured access or a provider outage still exposes or stops the service.

quiz.q: Why is an egress charge a cost risk and not a security risk?
quiz.a: It changes the bill, not who can read the data. Security risk covers breach, hijack, insecure interface or denial of service.

quiz.q: Match two benefits to the risks they create and give one mitigation for each.
quiz.a: Capex to opex creates bill shock; mitigate with budgets and alerts. Global reach creates data-location risk; mitigate by choosing a region and writing it into the contract.

quiz.q: List three common cloud threat types.
quiz.a: Data breach, account hijack, insecure interface (or denial of service).

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry this ledger becomes FinOps, where budgets and alerts sit beside security controls. Researchers study lock-in through portability benchmarks and data-sovereignty law. Search for cloud exit strategy, egress pricing and tenant isolation if you want the practitioner view.
